task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exorbitant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exorbitant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The beach kiosk wanted an exorbitant twelve dollars for a single scoop of ice cream, and somehow the line never shortened.
Overpriced stops short of exorbitant — an overpriced ticket costs somewhat more than it should, while an exorbitant one has left the orbit of fair pricing altogether.
Extortionate goes further than exorbitant — it adds an accusation: the seller is treating your desperation as the price tag.

Steep is the informal word for a price that stings — what you mutter at the register before paying anyway. Exorbitant is the formal accusation: the number has lost any relation to fairness, and calling it that is a charge, not a grumble. A steep price still gets paid; an exorbitant one gets protested.

Outrageous is the all-purpose cry of protest at anything that violates decency — prices, behavior, decisions alike. Exorbitant is narrower and more exact: it belongs to prices, rates, and demands, and its specific charge is that the number sits unreasonably far past fair. Every exorbitant bill is outrageous; most outrageous things involve no bill at all.

Exorbitant means excessive, unreasonably high.

When the ferry broke down, the island's one taxi driver quoted stranded visitors an exorbitant two hundred dollars for the six-mile ride to the hotel — a figure with no relation to fuel, to time, or to any fair rate.
Exorbitant does more than say a price is high — it says the price has left the orbit of reason entirely, so far beyond fair that naming it out loud feels like an insult.
Exorbitant is the complaint you file in writing; steep is what you mutter at the register.
Both mean overpriced, but exorbitant carries indignation and a claim of unreasonableness — use it when the number is not just high but indefensible.

The new owners saw it differently: theirs was the only boat, and the fare tripled in a single season.
